So you say «الزيدون هم الأفضلون والأفاضل» and «الهندات هنَّ الفُضْلَياتُ» and «الفُضُل». As for his saying «it is not pluralised unless annexed», its pluralisation is not then determined; rather, if it is annexed to an indefinite, its pluralisation is not allowed, and if annexed to a definite, both plural and singular are allowed."

semin-durr:6-6.t: His saying: {لَتُلَقَّى}: «لَقِيَ» in the light form takes one object, and with doubling takes two; the first of the two here was made to stand in the place of the agent, and the second is «القرآنَ». The statement of one who said that its original is «تَلَقَّنَ» with nūn / is an interpretation of meaning, so nothing is attached to it, for the nūn was replaced by a weak letter.

semin-durr:7-7.t:
His saying: {إِذْ قَالَ}: It may be accusative by implying "remember" or "know", indicated by «عَليم» or «حَليم». There is weakness in this, because the attribute is restricted by this adverbial.
His saying: {بِشِهَابٍ قَبَسٍ}: The Kufans read it with tanwīn on «شهاب», on the basis that «قَبَساً» is a badal from «شهاب» or an adjective of it, because it has the meaning of «مَقْبوس» (taken), like al-qabaḍ and al-naqaḍ. The others read it by annexation, in explanation, because a shihāb may be a qabas or something else. Al-shihāb is the flame. Al-qabas is a piece of it, whether on a stick or not. And «أَوْ» is in its ordinary sense of classification. The ṭāʾ in «تَصْطَلُون» is a replacement for the tāʾ of the form ifʿitāl, because it is from «صَلِيَ بالنار».

semin-durr:8-8.t:
His saying: {نُودِيَ}: There are three possibilities for what stands in the place of the agent. The first: that it is the pronoun of Mūsā, and it is the apparent one. In that case there are three possibilities for «أَنْ». The first: that it is the explicative (mufassira), because what has the meaning of saying precedes. The second: that it is the particle governing the imperfect, but here connected with the past; and the detailed treatment of that has been covered, on the basis of removal of the preposition, i.e. "Mūsā was called with: 'Blessed is…'". The third: that it is the lightened one (from inna), its ism being the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) and «بُوْرِك» its khabar; and there is no need here for a separator, because it is a supplication; and the like has been covered in Sūrat al-Nūr at His saying {أَنْ غَضِب} [al-Nūr: 9] in the reading of it as a past verb.
Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: may it be the one lightened from the heavy, the implied form being «بأنَّه بُورك», the pronoun being the pronoun of the matter and the story? I say: No, because «قد» is required. If you ask: what about implying it? I say: that is not sound, because it is a marker and is not omitted." End. So he prevented its being the lightened one for what was mentioned, and this is built on his view that «بُوْرِكَ» is a statement, not a supplication. But if we say that it is a supplication, as was covered in al-Nūr, there is no need for a separator, as covered. There was a difficulty raised about it: that a request does not occur as a khabar in this chapter, so how does this occur as the khabar of the lightened «أَنْ» when it is a supplication? The second of the first possibilities: that what stands in the place of the agent is «أَنْ بُوْرِكَ» itself, by omission of the preposition, i.e. «بأَنْ بُوْرِكَ». And «أَنْ» in that case is either the governing one originally, or the lightened one.
The third: that it is the pronoun of the maṣdar understood from the verb, i.e. "the call was called", then explained by what follows it. Like it is {ثُمَّ بَدَا لَهُمْ مِّن بَعْدِ مَا رَأَوُاْ الآيات لَيَسْجُنُنَّهُ} [Yūsuf: 35].
His saying: {مَن فِي النار}: «مَنْ» stands in the place of the agent of «بُوْرك». And bāraka takes its object directly, and for that reason it was built in the passive. One says «بارَكَكَ اللهُ», «بارَكَ عليكَ», «بارَكَ فيك» and «بارك لكَ». The poet said:
3539 - فَبُوْرِكْتَ مَوْلُوداً وبُوْرِكْتَ ناشِئاً ... وبُوْرِكْتَ عند الشِّيْب إذ أَنْتَ أَشْيَبُ
(You were blessed as a newborn, blessed as a youth, and blessed in old age when you turned grey.)
And ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr said:
3540 - فبُوْرِكَ في بَنِيْكَ وفي بَنيهمْ ... إذا ذُكِروا ونحن لك الفِداءُ
(May there be blessing in your sons and their sons whenever they are mentioned, and we are a ransom for you.)
And another said:
3541 - بُوْرِك الميِّتُ الغرِيبُ كما بُوْ ... رِكَ نَضْحُ الرُّمانِّ والزيتونِ
(Blessed be the dead stranger, as the sprinkling of pomegranate and olive was blessed.)
What is meant by «مَنْ» is either the Creator the Exalted, with an omitted muḍāf, i.e. "He whose power and authority is in the fire". It is also said: what is meant is Mūsā and the angels, and likewise «ومَنْ حولَها». It is also said: what is meant by «مَنْ» is the non-rational, which is the light and the places around it.
His saying: {وَسُبْحَانَ الله}: There are several possibilities. The first: that it completes the call, i.e. he was called with blessing and with the glorification of the Lord of Might; i.e. he was called with the two things together. The second: that it is the speech of Allah the Exalted addressing our Prophet Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and on this it is a parenthesis within the course of the story. The third: that its meaning is "and blessed is he who glorified Allah". He means that he omitted «مَنْ» and its ṣila and kept the object of the ṣila, the implied form being: "blessed is he who is in the fire and he who is around it, and he who said: Glory be to Allah". And «سُبْحانَ» in reality is not the object of «قال», but of a verb from its own word, and that verb is what is made accusative by the saying.

semin-durr:9-9.t:
His saying: {إِنَّهُ أَنَا الله}: There are two views on the ism of «إنَّ». The more apparent: that it is the pronoun of the matter; {أَنَا الله} is a mubtadaʾ and its khabar, and {العزيز الحكيم} are two adjectives of Allah. The second: that it is a pronoun referring to what is indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "the one speaking to you is I", and «الله» is an explication (bayān) of «أنا», and «الله العزيز الحكيم» are two adjectives for the explication. Al-Zamakhsharī said this. The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "When the agent is omitted and the verb built in the passive, the pronoun may not refer to that / omitted one, since the verb has been changed from its construction for it, and it has been resolved that it not be spoken about; so a pronoun referring to it contradicts that, as it would become something cared about."
I say: there is something to consider in this, because attention may be turned to it. That was covered in al-Baqara at His saying {فَمَنْ عُفِيَ لَهُ} [verse 178], then He said «وأداءٌ إليه», and it was said: i.e. the one who pardoned, who is the guardian of the blood, as its analysis has preceded. And even if that is conceded, al-Zamakhsharī did not say that it refers to that agent; he said only: it refers to what is indicated by what precedes it, meaning from the context.
Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "It may be the pronoun of «رَبّ», i.e. 'the Lord is I, Allah', so «أنا» would be a separating pronoun (faṣl), or emphasis, or the khabar of «إنَّ», with «الله» a badal from it."

semin-durr:10-10.t:
His saying: {وَأَلْقِ}: It is conjoined to the preceding nominal declarative clause. It has already been covered that Sībawayh does not require agreement of clauses and allows «جاء زيدٌ ومَنْ أبوك» ("Zayd came, and who is your father?"), and his proofs were covered at the beginning of al-Baqara. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: to what is His saying {وَأَلْقِ عَصَاكَ} conjoined? I say: to His saying «بُوْرِكَ», for the meaning is: he was called, 'Blessed is…', and it was said to him: 'Cast down your staff.' The proof of that is His saying «وأَنْ أَلْقِ عَصاك» after His saying «يا موسى إنَّه أنا اللهُ», with repetition of the explicative particle, as you say «كتْبْتُ إليه أَنْ حُجَّ واعْتَمِرْ» ('I wrote to him: perform Hajj and perform ʿUmra'), or if you wish «أَنْ حُجَّ وأَنِ اعْتَمِرْ»." The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "His saying that it is conjoined to «بُوْرِكَ» contradicts his assumption «وقيل له: أَلْقِ عصاك», because this is a clause conjoined to «بُوْرِكَ», and the part of it that is the object of «وقيل» is not itself conjoined to «بُوْرِكَ». He needed to imply 'and it was said to him: Cast' only so that it would be a declarative clause suited to the declarative clause to which it was conjoined. It is as though he sees in conjunction the agreement of the conjoined clauses; but the correct view is that this is not required." Then he mentioned the position of Sībawayh.
His saying: {تَهْتَزُّ}: a ḥāl clause from the hāʾ of «تَراها», because the seeing is visual.
His saying: {كَأَنَّهَا جَآنٌّ}: It may be a second ḥāl, or a ḥāl from the pronoun of «تَهْتَزُّ», making it a nested ḥāl. Al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read «جَأَنٌّ» with hamza in place of the alif; the explanation of this was covered at the end of al-Fātiḥa at {وَلاَ الضآلين} [al-Fātiḥa: 7].
His saying: {وَلَمْ يُعَقِّبْ}: It may be conjoined to «ولى», or it may be another ḥāl. The meaning: he did not turn back on his heel. Like his saying:
3542 - فما عَقَّبوا إذ قيلَ: هل مَنْ مُعَقِّبٍ ... ولا نَزَلُوا يومَ الكَريهةِ مَنْزِلا
(They did not turn back when it was said, "Is there anyone to turn back?", nor did they dismount at any stopping place on the day of battle.)

semin-durr:11-11.t:
His saying: {إَلاَّ مَن ظَلَمَ}: There are two views on it. The first: it is a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), because the messengers are protected from sins. This is the apparent, correct view. The second: that it is connected. The exegetes have statements about it which this is not the place for. From al-Farrāʾ: it is connected, but from an omitted sentence, whose implied form is: "Only others fear, except one who has done wrong." Al-Naḥḥās rejected it, saying: were this allowed, «لا أضرب القوم إلاَّ زيداً» would be allowed, meaning "I strike only others, except Zayd"; and this is the opposite of clarity and brings what has no known meaning.
Al-Zamakhsharī implied «لكن» ("but"), which is the sign that it is disconnected, and he mentioned a lengthy discussion. On the disconnected reading it is accusative only, in the dialect of the Hijaz. In the dialect of Tamīm both accusative and nominative are allowed, the nominative as a badal from the agent before it. On the connected reading, both are allowed in both dialects, and the preferred is the badal, because the speech is not affirmative.
Abū Jaʿfar and Zayd ibn Aslam read «ألا» with fatḥa on the hamza and light lām, making it a particle of alerting. And «مَنْ» is conditional, its apodosis {فَإِنِّي غَفُورٌ}.
The majority read «حُسْناً» with tanwīn. Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā al-Aṣbahānī read it without tanwīn, making it a maṣdar on the pattern fuʿlā like ruj‘ā, and so he made it a diptote because of the alif of femininity. Ibn Miqsam read it with ḍamma on the ḥāʾ and the sīn, with tanwīn. Mujāhid and Abū Ḥaywa, and it is also reported from Abū ʿAmr, read it with fatḥa on both. The explanation of the two readings has been covered in al-Baqara.

semin-durr:12-12.t:
His saying: {تَخْرُجْ}: The apparent sense is that it is the jawāb (response) of His saying «أَدْخِلْ», i.e. "if you insert it, it will come out in this condition". It was also said that there is an omission in the speech, whose implied form is: "Insert your hand, it will enter, and bring it out, it will come out"; so he omitted from the second what he stated in the first, and from the first what he stated in the second. This is an implied form with no need for it.
His saying: {بَيْضَآءَ}: a ḥāl from the agent of «تَخْرُجْ». And {مِنْ غَيْرِ سواء} may be another ḥāl, or from the pronoun in «بَيْضاء», or a naʿt of «بَيْضاءَ».
His saying: {فِي تِسْعِ}: There are several possibilities. The first: that it is a third ḥāl. Abū l-Baqāʾ said it, meaning from the agent of «يَخْرُجْ» / i.e. "a sign among nine signs". So he assumed it. The second: that it is attached to an omitted element, i.e. "go with nine". Al-Zamakhsharī's preference for that has already been covered at the beginning of this subject, where the basmala was mentioned, and he compared it to the saying of another:
3543 - وقُلْتُ إلى الطَعامِ فقالَ منهم ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(And I said, "To the food!", and one of them said...)
and their saying «بالرَّفاهِ والبنين» ("with harmony and sons"), and he considered this assumption the clearer and better. The third: that it is attached to His saying «وأَلْقِ عَصاكَ وأَدْخِلْ». Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The meaning may be: 'Cast your staff and insert your hand among nine signs', i.e. in the total of nine signs. A speaker may say: the signs were eleven, two of them being the hand and the staff. And the nine are: the splitting (of the sea), the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration, the drought in their desert regions, and the shortage in their fields." End. On this basis «في» has the meaning of «مع» ("with"), because the hand and the staff are then outside the nine. Ibn ʿAṭiyya did likewise, that is, he made «في تِسْع» connected to «أَلْقِ» and «أَدْخِلْ», except that he made the hand and the staff part of the nine. He said: "The implied form is: We pave the way for you in that, and We ease [it] among nine."
Al-Zajjāj made «في» mean «مِنْ». He said: "As you say: 'Take for me, of the camels, ten, among them two stallions', i.e. two stallions of them."
His saying: {إلى فِرْعَوْنَ}: This is attached to what «في تسعِ» is attached to, if you do not make it a ḥāl. If we make it a ḥāl we attach it to an omitted element, which Abū l-Baqāʾ implied as «مُرْسَلاً إلى فرعون» ("sent to Pharaoh"). There is something to consider in that, because it is a restricted "being" (kawn muqayyad), and al-Zajjāj preceded him in this assumption; it is as though both intended to explain the meaning, not the grammatical analysis. Abū l-Baqāʾ also allowed it to be a naʿt of «آيات» and implied «واصلةً إلى فرعونَ» ("reaching Pharaoh"). In it is what was mentioned.

semin-durr:13-13.t: His saying: {مُبْصِرَةً}: a ḥāl. The seeing is ascribed to it figuratively, because by it one sees. It is also said: rather it is from abṣara, made transitive with hamza from baṣira, i.e. it makes others see because of the clarity in it; but this is another figure, different from the first. It is also said: it has the meaning of a passive participle, like «ماءٌ دافِقٌ», i.e. «مَدْفُوق» (poured). ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn and Qatāda read it with fatḥa on the mīm and the ṣād, i.e. on the pattern of «أَرْضٌ مَسْبَعَةٌ» (a land with predators), and its accusative is also as a ḥāl; and Abū l-Baqāʾ made it, in this reading, [an object of purpose; and that has already been covered].

semin-durr:14-14.t:
His saying: {واستيقنتهآ}: This clause may be conjoined to the preceding clause. It may be a ḥāl from the agent of «جَحَدُوا», and this is stronger in blame. And istafʿala here has the meaning of tafaʿʿala, as in istaʿẓama and istakbara, meaning taʿaẓẓama and takabbara.
His saying: {ظُلْماً وَعُلُوّاً}: Both may be in the position of ḥāl, i.e. "wrongdoing and exalting themselves", or both may be objects of purpose, i.e. what drove that was wrongdoing and arrogance. ʿAbd Allāh (ibn Masʿūd), Ibn Waththāb, al-Aʿmash and Ṭalḥa read «وعِليَّاً» with kasra on the ʿayn and the lām, turning the wāw into yāʾ. Its explanation has been covered at «عِتيَّا» in Maryam. It is also reported from al-Aʿmash and Ibn Waththāb with ḍamma on the ʿayn as in «عِتيّا». It was also read «غُلُوَّاً» with the dotted ghayn, which is close to this meaning.
His saying: {كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ}: «كيف» is a fronted khabar and «عاقبةُ» its ism, the clause being in the accusative position by removal of the preposition, because it is suspended from «انْظُرْ» with the meaning "reflect".

semin-durr:15-15.t: His saying: {وَقَالاَ}: Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask: is not this the place for fāʾ rather than wāw, as in your saying «أَعْطَيْتُه فَشَكر» ("I gave him and so he thanked") and «مَنَعْتُه فَصَبرَ» ("I withheld from him and so he was patient")? I say: Yes, but conjoining it with wāw gives the sense that what they said was part of what the giving of knowledge produced in them and something of its requirements; so he left that implied and then conjoined praise to it, as though he said: "We gave them knowledge and they acted upon it, and they taught it and knew it with true knowledge, and they said: Praise be to Allah." End. «عِلْماً» was made indefinite only for magnification, i.e. exalted knowledge, or as an indication of partiality, because it is very little in relation to His, the Exalted's, knowledge.

semin-durr:17-17.t:
His saying: {مِنَ الجن}: and what follows it is an explanation of his troops, so it is attached to an omitted element. It is also possible that this prepositional phrase is a ḥāl, and so is attached to an omitted element too.
His saying: {يُوزَعُونَ}: i.e. they are restrained and held back. Al-wazʿ is restraining and confining. One says «وَزَعَه يَزَعُهُ», so he is wāziʿ and mawzūʿ. ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "What the ruler restrains is more than what the Qurʾān restrains." And from him: / "The judge must have a restrainer (wazaghah)."
The poet said:
3544 - ومَن لم يَزَعْه لُبُّه وحَياؤُه ... فليس له مِنْ شَيْبِ فَوْدَيْه وازِعُ
(Whoever is not restrained by his reason and modesty has no restraint in the grey of his temples.)
And His saying {أوزعني أَنْ أَشكُرَ} has the meaning "inspire me", from this; for its verification is "make me restrain myself from disbelief".
[Translator's note: the source gives «يَزَغُ» and «وَزَغَةٍ» with ghayn in the sayings of ʿUthmān where «يَزَعُ» and «وَزَعَةٍ» with ʿayn would be expected from the root; translated here as written in the source, in the sense of "restrain".]

semin-durr:19-19.t:
His saying: {ضَاحِكاً}: It is said: it is a confirming ḥāl (ḥāl muʾakkida), because it is understood from «تَبَسَّمَ». It is also said: rather it is an anticipated ḥāl (ḥāl muqaddara), for smiling is the beginning of laughing. It is also said: since smiling can be from anger, from which is «he smiled the smile of an angry man», he brought «ضاحكاً» to clarify it. ʿAntara said:
3550 - لمَّا رآني قد قَصَدْت أُرِيْدُه ... أبدى نواجِذَه لِغَيْرِ تَبَسُّمِ
(When he saw that I had made for him, wanting him, he bared his back teeth, not in a smile.)
And «تَبَسَّمَ» is on the pattern tafaʿʿala, with the meaning of the simple basama. He said:
3551 - وتَبْسِمُ عن ألمى كأن مُنَوَّراً ... تَخَلَّلَ حُرَّ الرَّمْلِ دِعْصٌ له نَدِي
(She smiles, showing dark-lipped gums, as if a blossoming flower had penetrated the pure sand, a dune moist with dew.)
And one of the later poets said:
3552 - كأنَّما تَبْسِمُ عن لؤلؤٍ ... مُنَضَّدٍ أو بَرَدٍ أو أَقَاحِ
(It is as if she smiles over strung pearls, or hailstones, or camomile flowers.)
Ibn al-Samayfaʿ read «ضَحِكاً» in the short form, and there are three possibilities for it. The first: that it is a confirming maṣdar of the meaning of «تَبَسَّم», because it has its meaning. The second: that it is in the position of ḥāl, so it is in meaning like the one before it. The third: that it is an active participle like fariḥa; that is because its verb is on faʿila with kasra on the ʿayn, which is intransitive, so it is like fariḥ and baṭir.
His saying: {أَنْ أَشْكُرَ}: the second object of «أَوْزِعْني», because its meaning is "inspire me". It is also said that its meaning is "make me restrain the thanking for Your blessing", i.e. hold it and prevent it so that it does not escape from me, so that I remain ever thankful. Al-Zajjāj's interpretation of it as "prevent me from disbelieving Your blessing" belongs to the category of interpreting the meaning by the necessary consequence.

semin-durr:20-20.t:
His saying: {مَالِيَ لاَ أَرَى الهدهد}: This is a question of inquiry (istifhām tawqīf), and there is no need to claim inversion (qalb), that the original is «ما للهدهد لا أراه؟» ("What is wrong with the hoopoe that I do not see it?"), since the meaning is strong without it. The hoopoe (al-hudhud) is well known. Its diminutive is «هُدَيْهِد», which is the analogical form. Some grammarians claimed that the yāʾ of its diminutive turns into alif, so one says «هُداهِد». He recited:
3553 - كهُداهِدٍ كَسَرَ الرماةُ جناحَه ... يَدْعو بقارعةِ الطريق هَدِيْلا
(Like a hudāhid whose wing the archers broke, calling "hadīl" at the roadside.)
as they said «دُوابَّة» and «شُوابَّة» for «دُوَيْبَّة» and «شُوَيْبَّة». Some rejected it, saying that al-hudāhid is the dove, abundant in vibrating its voice. The Arabs claim that a bird of prey, in the time of the Flood, snatched a chick of a dove called al-Hadīl. They said: every dove that cries is crying only for al-Hadīl.
His saying: {أَمْ كَانَ}: This is the disconnected «أم» (am munqaṭiʿa), and the discussion of it has been covered. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "His saying «مالي لا أرى الهدهد»: the aim of the speech is: the hoopoe is absent; but he took the necessary consequence of its absence, which is that he does not see it, and inquired about it as a halt at the consequence; and this is a kind of concision. The interrogative in His saying «مالي» takes the place of the hamza that «أم» needs." The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "The apparent sense of his words is that «أم» is connected (muttaṣila) and that the interrogative in His saying «مالي» takes the place of the interrogative hamza. So the meaning is: has it been absent from me just now, so I did not see it at the time of inspection, or was it among those who were absent before, and I did not notice its absence?" I say: this should not be thought of Abū Muḥammad, for he is not ignorant that the condition of the connected «أم» is the prior occurrence of the interrogative hamza or of equalization, not just any interrogative.

semin-durr:21-21.t:
His saying: {عَذَاباً}: i.e. taʿdhīban; so it is a noun of maṣdar, or a maṣdar with the augments removed, like {أَنبَتَكُمْ مِّنَ الأرض نَبَاتاً} [Nūḥ: 17]. They wrote «أو لأَاذْبَحَنَّه» with an additional alif between the lām-alif and the dhāl; it may not be read with it. This is as was covered, that they wrote «ولأَاوْضَعوا خلالَكم» with an additional alif between the lām-alif and the wāw.
His saying: {أَوْ لَيَأْتِيَنِّي}: Ibn Kathīr read it with the doubled nūn of emphasis followed by the nūn of protection (nūn al-wiqāya). This is the original, and he followed, besides, the orthography of his codex. The others read it with a single doubled nūn only. The more apparent is that it is the heavy nūn of emphasis, joined by its kasra to the yāʾ of the first person. It is also said: rather it is the light nūn of emphasis assimilated into the nūn of protection; but this is nothing, because of the difference from the two verbs before it. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read it with a doubled nūn with fatḥa, not joining it to the yāʾ.

semin-durr:23-23.t:
His saying: {وَأُوتِيَتْ}: It may be conjoined to «تَمْلِكُهم». The conjoining of a past to an imperfect is allowed because the imperfect has its meaning, i.e. «مَلَكَتْهُمْ». It may also be in the accusative position as a ḥāl from the nominative pronoun of «تَمْلِكُهم», with «قد» implied with it according to those who hold that.
His saying: {مِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ}: general but specified by reason, because she was not given what Sulaymān was given.
His saying: {وَلَهَا عَرْشٌ}: This may be a clause independent in itself, brought to report it; or conjoined to «أُوتِيَتْ»; or a ḥāl from the nominative pronoun of «أُوتِيَتْ». The best is that the ḥāl be the prepositional phrase, with «عَرْشٌ» nominative by it. Some pause at «عَرْشٌ», cutting it off from its adjective. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Among the fools of the storytellers are those who pause at His saying {وَلَهَا عَرْشٌ} then begin «عظيمٌ وَجَدْتُها», meaning 'a great thing, that I found her'; fleeing from the hoopoe's regarding her throne as great, he fell into a great matter, which is the distortion of the Book of Allah." I say: al-nawkā are the foolish, plural of anwak. What he mentioned about the matter of pausing was reported by al-Dānī from Nāfiʿ, and he affirmed it, as did Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī, who traced it to some of the people of knowledge, so it should not be said "fools of the storytellers". Al-Dānī analysed it as «عظيم» being a mubtadaʾ and «وَجَدْتُها» the khabar. This is a mistake: how can one begin with an indefinite without a justification, and report about it with a clause having no link between it and the subject? The grammatical analysis is what al-Zamakhsharī said: that «عظيماً» is an adjective of an omitted element that is a fronted khabar [and «وَجَدْتُها» is a postponed mubtadaʾ with a maṣdar particle implied with it, i.e. "a great matter is my finding her and her people not worshipping Allah the Exalted."
[Translator's note: the bracket opened in the source at the last sentence is not closed in the Arabic text.]

semin-durr:18-18.t:
His saying: {حتى إِذَآ}: There are two views on what is bounded by «حتى». The first: it is «يُوْزَعُون», because it implies the meaning: "they march, some of them being prevented from leaving others, until when". The second: that it is omitted, i.e. "so they marched until". The discussion of «حتى» entering «إذا» has been covered: is it a particle of commencement or a preposition?
His saying: «وادي» is attached to «أَتَوْا». It was made to take «على» only because that is what actually occurred, for they were carried on the wind, so they were above it. It is also said: it is from their saying «أَتَيْتُ عليه» when you exhaust it to its end; the meaning is that they traversed the whole valley and reached its end.
All the readers paused at «وادِ» without the yāʾ, following the orthography, and because it is dropped in pronunciation due to the meeting of two quiescent letters in connected speech, and because it is dropped even where it is not dropped for the meeting of two quiescent letters, as in {جَابُواْ الصخر بالواد} [al-Fajr: 9]; so dropping it in pausing, when its dropping without the meeting of two quiescents is a known thing, is more fitting. Except al-Kisāʾī, who paused with the yāʾ. He said: "Because what required the dropping was only the meeting of two quiescents in connected speech, and that has gone, so the lām (of the word) returned," and he excused his departure from the orthography by the strength of the original.
Al-naml (ants) is a well-known generic noun; its singular is namla. One says also numla and numl with ḍamma on the nūn and sukūn on the mīm, numula and numul with two ḍammas, namula with fatḥa then ḍamma, on the pattern of samura, and namul on the pattern of rajul. Its derivation is from tanammul because of the abundance of its movement. From it the informer is called al-munmil; one says «أَنْمَلَ بين القومِ يُنْمِلُ», i.e. he informed and slandered, because of the abundance of his going back and forth and moving in that. He said:
3545 - ولَسْتُ بذي نَيْرَبٍ فيهمُ ... ولا مُنْمِشٍ فيهمُ مُنْمِلُ
(I am not one of mischief among them, nor an instigator among them, a slanderer.)
One also says «نَمَل يَنْمُلُ», so he is namil and nammāl. «تَنَمَّل القوم» means the people dispersed, as in gathering, with the dispersal of ants. In the proverb: «أجمعُ مِنْ نملة» ("More gathering than an ant"). Al-namla is also a vent that comes out on the side, likened to it in shape; al-namla is also a split in the hoof, from which: «فَرَسٌ مَنْمولُ القوائم». And al-anmula, the tip of the finger, is from that because of its fineness and the speed of its movement; the plural is anāmil.
His saying: {قَالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ}: This ant here is truly feminine, by the evidence of the sign of the feminine being attached to its verb. For namla is used for the male and the female; so when a distinction is intended, one says "a male ant" and "a female ant", like ḥamāma and yamāma. Al-Zamakhsharī related from Abū Ḥanīfa, may Allah be pleased with him, that he came upon Qatāda saying "Ask me", and told someone to ask him about Sulaymān's ant: was it male or female? He did not answer. Abū Ḥanīfa was asked about that, and he said: It was female. He argued from the attachment of the sign. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "That is because namla is like ḥamāma and shāh (sheep), in that they are applied to both male and female, so a distinction is made between them by a sign, as in their saying: a male ḥamāma and a female ḥamāma, and 'he' and 'she'." End.
But the Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) rejected this and said: "The attachment of the tāʾ in «قالَتْ» does not indicate that the ant is feminine; rather it is correct to say of the male «قالت نملة», because namla, even though it has the tāʾ, is among those in which the male is not distinguished from the female; and whatever is so, like the ant and the louse, among animals where between its plural and its singular is the tāʾ of the feminine, is predicated of with the predication of the feminine, and its being predicated of with the feminine does not indicate that it is male or female; for the tāʾ entered it to distinguish, not to indicate true femininity, but indicating the single one of this genus." He said: "Qatāda was well versed in Arabic. His being silenced indicates his knowledge of the language, since he knew that the ant is predicated of with the feminine, even though it is applied to the female and the male, as neither can be distinguished in it. The attachment of the sign does not indicate; so masculinity and femininity are known only by revelation from Allah the Exalted." He said: "As for deducing its femininity from the Book of Allah by «قالَتْ», and that had it been male it would have been said «قال», the speech of the grammarians is against it, and that it is predicated of only with the feminine, whether male or female." He said: "As for al-Zamakhsharī's likening / the ant to the dove and the sheep, in them there is a shared measure in which the male is distinguished from the female, so one can say a male ḥamāma and a female ḥamāma, with the distinction by adjective; as for distinguishing by 'he' and 'she', it is not allowed. You do not say 'he is the ḥamāma' nor 'he is the shāh'. As for the ant and the louse, in them the male is not distinguished from the female, so only the feminine is permissible in predication, and its ruling is that of the tāʾ-feminine among animals like al-marʾa, or non-rational like al-dābba, unless a separation occurs between the verb and what it is predicated of, in which case the sign may be attached or not attached, as established in the science of Arabic." End.
As for what he mentioned, there is something to consider in it: femininity is either verbal (lafẓī) or semantic (maʿnawī). The verbal is not considered at all in attaching the sign, by the evidence that «قامَتْ رَبْعةُ» is not allowed when you mean a man; for that reason «قامت طلحةُ» and «حمزةُ» are not allowed for two masculine proper names. So the attachment must be only for semantic femininity. The verbal form of femininity and masculinity is determined in the chapter on number in a special sense as well: that we look at how the Arabs treat that word in masculine or feminine, without regard to its signification; so there this consideration applies. To verify it here would take us away from the purpose, and I have only alerted you to the amount needed.
As for his saying "As for the ant and the louse, they are not distinguished", meaning one cannot arrive at knowing the male or female of them, unlike the dove and the sheep for which learning of that is possible, that too is not conceded: learning of that may be possible, and learning of the maleness of a dove and sheep is easier than learning of the maleness of an ant and a louse. And his prohibiting the saying "he is the sheep" and "he is the dove" is also not conceded.
Al-Ḥasan, Ṭalḥa and Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān read «النَّمُل» and «نَمُلة» with ḍamma on the mīm and fatḥa on the nūn, on the pattern of rajul and samura. And Sulaymān al-Taymī read both with two ḍammas. It has been covered that these are dialectal variants in the singular and plural.
His saying: {لاَ يَحْطِمَنَّكُمْ}: There are two views on it. The first: that it is a prohibition. The second: that it is the jawāb (response) to the command. If it is a prohibition there are two views: the first, that it is a resumptive prohibition having no grammatical connection with what precedes it; it is a prohibition to the troops in wording, and in meaning to the ants, i.e. "do not be in a position where they would crush you", like their saying «لا أُرَيَنَّك ههنا» ("Let me not see you here"). The second: that it is a badal for the clause of the command before it, which is «ادْخلوا». Al-Zamakhsharī addressed that, saying: "If you ask: what is «لا يَحْطِمَنَّكم»? I say: it may be a response to the command, and it may be a prohibition as a badal from the command. What allows it to be a badal is that it has the meaning: do not be where you are, lest they crush you, in the manner of «لا أُرَيَنَّك ههنا»; she meant: let not Sulaymān's troops crush you, and she brought what is more eloquent. Like it is «عَجِبْتُ من نفسي ومن إشْفاقِها» ('I marvelled at myself and at its solicitude')." The Shaykh said: "As for his analysis of it as a response to the command, it can be only on the reading of al-Aʿmash, since it is jussive there, although it may be a resumptive prohibition." I say: he means that al-Aʿmash read «لا يَحْطِمْكم» with sukūn on the mīm without the nūn of emphasis.
He said: "But with the presence of the nūn of emphasis that is not allowed except in poetry, and if that is not allowed in the response to a condition except in poetry, then it is more fitting that it not be allowed in the response to a command except in poetry. Its being a response to a command is disputed, as established in the science of grammar. An example of the nūn coming in the response to a condition is the poet's saying:
3546 - نَبَتُّمْ نباتَ الخَيْزُرانةِ في الثَّرَى ... حديثاً متى يأتِك الخيرُ يَنْفَعا
(You grew like the cane in the damp earth, recently; whenever good comes to you it benefits.)
and the saying of another:
3547 - فمهما تَشَأْ منه فَزارةُ تُعطِكُمْ ... ومهما تَشَأْ منه فَزارةُ تَمْنعا
(Whatever you wish from it, Fazāra gives you; and whatever you wish from it, Fazāra withholds.)
Sībawayh said: 'It is rare, in poetry; they likened it to the prohibition in that it is jussive and not obligatory.'" He said: "As for the analysis of it as a badal, it is not allowed, because the signification of «لا يَحْطِمَنَّكم» differs from that of «ادْخُلوا». As for his saying that it has the meaning: do not be where you are, lest they crush you, it is an interpretation of meaning, not of grammar / and the badal is a matter of the description of words. Yes, if the Qurʾānic wording were 'do not be where they would not crush you', the badal could be imagined in it, because the command to enter the dwellings is a prohibition from being on the surface of the earth. As for his saying 'that she meant: let not the troops of Sulaymān crush you, etc.', it allows an addition of nouns, which is not allowed; rather the apparent sense is the ascription of the ruling to Sulaymān and his troops. It is with an omitted muḍāf, i.e. the cavalry of Sulaymān and his troops, or the like, whichever assumption is sound." End.
As for his preventing its being the response to a command because of the nūn, Abū l-Baqāʾ preceded him in it, saying: "It is weak, because the response to a condition is not emphasized with the nūn in the preferred usage."
As for his preventing the badal by what he mentioned, we do not concede a difference of signification with respect to what the meaning comes to. As for his saying "it allows addition of nouns", he did not allow that; he only interpreted the meaning, and even on that assumption it has been said. The address in her saying «ادْخُلوا» came like the address of rational beings since they were treated as such.
Ubayy read «ادْخُلْنَ», «مَساكِنَكُنَّ», «لا يَحْطِمَنْكُنَّ» with the light nūn, bringing it in its original form. Shahr ibn Ḥawshab read «مَسْكَنَكُمْ» in the singular. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Qatāda and ʿĪsā al-Hamdānī read it with ḍamma on the yāʾ, fatḥa on the ḥāʾ, and shadda on the ṭāʾ and the nūn, the imperfect of ḥaṭṭamahu with shadda. From al-Ḥasan also are two readings: fatḥa on the yāʾ and shadda on the ṭāʾ, with sukūn on the ḥāʾ or kasra. The original is «لا يَحْتَطِمَنَّكم», which was assimilated. The sukūn on the ḥāʾ is problematic, and its like was covered in «لا يَهِدِّي» and its like. Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and Abū ʿAmr in one transmission read it with sukūn on the nūn of emphasis.
His saying: {وَهُمْ لاَ يَشْعُرُونَ}: a ḥāl clause. Al-ḥaṭm is breaking. One says «حَطَمْتُه فحَطِمَ»; then it was used for every extreme breaking. Al-ḥuṭām is what is broken by dryness, and it came to predominate for trivial things. Al-ḥuṭam is the swift driver, as though he breaks the camels. He said:
3548 - قد لَفَّها الليلُ بسَوَّاقٍ حُطَمْ ... ليس براعي إبِلٍ ولا غَنَمْ
ولا بَجَزَّارٍ على ظهرِ وَضَمْ
(Night has enveloped them with a harsh driver, no shepherd of camels nor of sheep, nor a butcher at a chopping block.)
Al-Ḥuṭama is one of the levels of the Fire. A man called ḥuṭama is a glutton, likening his belly to the Fire, as in his saying: 3549 - كأنمَّا في جَوْفِه تَنُّوْرُ ... (as if in his belly there were an oven…)
[Translator's note: the source text of the last verse is cut off after the first hemistich.]

semin-durr:22-22.t:
His saying: {فَمَكَثَ}: ʿĀṣim read it with fatḥa on the kāf; the others with ḍamma. They are two dialectal forms, except that the fatḥa is better known, and for that reason the adjective came as «ماكِث» and not «مَكِيْث». An excuse is made for it: that fāʿil has come for faʿula with ḍamma, such as ḥamuḍa, so it is ḥāmiḍ; khathura, so it is khāthir; and faruha, so it is fārih.
His saying: {غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ}: It may be an adjective of the maṣdar, i.e. "a stay not long", of time, i.e. "a time not long", and of place, i.e. "a place not far". The apparent sense is that the pronoun in «مكث» refers to the hoopoe. It is also said: to Sulaymān, peace be upon him.
His saying: {مِن سَبَإٍ}: Al-Bazzī and Abū ʿAmr read it with fatḥa on the hamza, making it the name of a tribe, or of a spot, and they made it a diptote because of being a proper name and feminine. On this is the poet's saying:
3554 - مِنْ سَبَأَ الحاضرينَ مَأْرِبَ إذ ... يَبْنُون مِنْ دونِ سَيْلِها العَرِما
(From Saba, the residents of Maʾrib, when they built the dam beyond its flood.)
Qunbul read it with sukūn on the hamza, as if he intended pausing and treated connected speech as pausing. The others read it with genitive and tanwīn, making it the name of the clan or the place. On this is the poet's saying:
3555 - الوارِدُون وتَيْمٌ في ذُرا سَبَأٍ ... قد عَضَّ أعناقََهم جِلْدُ الجواميسِ
(Those who come to water, with Taym in the heights of Saba, the hides of buffaloes having bitten into their necks.)
This disagreement applies identically in Sūrat Sabaʾ. In His saying {مِن سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ} there is of the rhetorical device (badīʿ) "paronomasia" (tajānus), namely inflectional paronomasia (tajnīs al-taṣrīf), which is an expression for each of two words being distinguished from the other by one letter, as in this verse. Like it is {تَفْرَحُونَ فِي الأرض بِغَيْرِ الحق وَبِمَا كُنتُمْ تَمْرَحُونَ} [Ghāfir: 75], and in the ḥadīth: «الخيلُ مَعْقُوْدٌ بنواصِيها الخيرُ» ("Good is tied to the forelocks of horses").
Another said:
3556 - للهِ ما صَنَعَتْ بنا ... تلك المَعاجِرُ والمحَاجِرْ
(By Allah, what those head-scarves and eye-sockets did to us!)
Al-Zamakhsharī said: "His saying {مِن سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ} is of the kind of speech the moderns call badīʿ. It is among the embellishments of speech connected with the wording, on condition that it comes naturally, or is made by one who knows the essence of speech and preserves with it the soundness and correctness of the meaning. Here it came with more than soundness, so it is beautiful and novel in wording and meaning. Do you not see that if «بخبر» were put in place of «بنَبَأ» the meaning would be sound, but as it came it is sounder, because of the additional element in naba' which accords with the description of the situation." He means by the addition that naba' is more specific than khabar, because it is said only of a report of consequence, whereas khabar is applied to what is of consequence and what is not, so every naba' is a khabar but not vice versa. Some express the like of {مِن سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ} in the science of badīʿ as "tardīd"; so said the author of al-Taḥrīr. Another said: tardīd is an expression for returning the ends of verses to their beginnings, or returning a word from the first half to the second half. An example of the first is his saying:
3557 - سَريعٌ إلى ابنِ العَمِّ يَلْطِمُ وَجْهَه ... وليس إلى داعي الخَنا بسَريعِ
(Quick toward his cousin to slap his face, but not quick toward one who calls to obscenity.)
and an example of the second his saying:
3558 - والليالي إذا نَأَيْتُمْ طِوالٌ ... والليالي إذا دَنَوْتُمْ قِصَارُ
(The nights, when you are far, are long; the nights, when you are near, are short.)
Ibn Kathīr in one transmission read «مِنْ سَبَاً» in the short form with tanwīn. From him also «مِنْ سَبْأَ» with sukūn on the bāʾ and fatḥa on the hamza, making it on the pattern faʿl and making it a diptote for the reason previously mentioned.
From al-Aʿmash: «مِنْ سَبْءِ» with a kasra on the hamza, without tanwīn. There is a difficulty in it, for there is no reason for building. What appears to me is that its tanwīn must be turned into a mīm in connected speech by necessity of its meeting the bāʾ, so the transmitter heard it and thought he had put kasra without tanwīn. It is reported from Abū ʿAmr «مِنْ سَبَا» with a clear alif, like their saying «تَفَرَّقُوا أَيْدِيْ سَبا» ("they scattered in all directions"). Likewise «بنَبَا» was read with a pure alif, and both should be from one reader.
Saba' was originally the name of a man from Qaḥṭān, whose name was ʿAbd Shams, and Saba' is a title of his. He was titled with it only because he was the first to take captives (sabā); ten children were born to him: six went right (tayāmana), namely Ḥimyar, Kinda, al-Azd, Ashʿar, Khathʿam and Bujayla; and four went left (tashāʾama), namely Lakhm, Judhām, ʿĀmila and Ghassān.

semin-durr:24-24.t:
His saying: {وَجَدتُّهَا}: This is the one meaning "I met" and "I came upon"; / so it takes one object, and «يَسْجُدون» is a ḥāl from its object and what is conjoined to it.
[Translator's note: the source text begins with a stray closing bracket "]" with no opening bracket; translated as the sense requires.]
His saying: {أَلاَّ يَسْجُدُواْ}: Al-Kisāʾī read «ألا» lightened, and the others with shadda. As for al-Kisāʾī's reading, «ألا» in it is an alert and an opening particle, and «يا» after it is a vocative particle or also an alerting particle, as will come, and «اسْجُدوا» is an imperative verb. The proper writing, on this reading, would be «يا اسْجُدوا», but the Companions dropped the alif of «يا» and the hamzat al-waṣl of «اسْجُدوا» in writing, as both dropped in pronunciation, and joined the yāʾ to the sīn of «اسْجُدوا», so its form became «يَسْجُدوا» as you see. Thus the two readings coincided in pronunciation and writing and differed in analysis.
The grammarians differed about this «يا»: is it a particle of alerting, or of vocative with the one addressed omitted, its implied form being "O you, prostrate"? That was covered at His saying {ياليتني} [verse 73] in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. The preferred is that it is for alerting, so that it does not lead to much omission without anything remaining to indicate the omitted. Do you not see that the vocative clause itself is omitted; so if you claimed omission of the one addressed, the omission would be great and no governed element would remain to indicate its governor, unlike when you make it for alerting. But here we face the objection that before it is another alerting particle, namely «ألا». An excuse was made for that: that the two were combined for emphasis. And if they combined two operative particles for emphasis, as in his saying:
3559 - فَأَصْبَحْنَ لا يَسْألْنَنِي عَنْ بما به ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(So they became such that they ask me not about that which is in it…)
then non-operative ones are all the more fitting. Moreover they have combined two operative particles identical in wording and meaning, as in his saying:
3560 - فلا واللهِ لا يلفى لِما بي ... ولا لِلِما بهم أبداً دَواءُ
(No, by Allah, no remedy is found for what is in me, nor ever for what is in them.)
So this is more fitting. And the direct attachment of «يا» to an imperative verb, with «ألا» of opening before it, is frequent, as in his saying:
3561 - ألا يا اسْلَمِي ثُمَّ اسْلمي ثُمَّتَ اسْلَمي ... ثلاثَ تحيَّاتٍ وإنْ لَمْ تَكَلَّمي
(O be safe, then be safe, then again be safe: three greetings, even if you do not speak.)
and his saying:
3562 - ألا يا اسْلَمِي يا دارَ مَيَّ على البِلى ... ولا زالَ مُنْهَلاًّ بجَرْعائِكِ القَطْرُ
(O be safe, abode of Mayy, despite decay, and may rain ever pour on your sandy plain.)
and his saying:
3563 - ألا يا اسلمي ذاتَ الدَّماليجِ والعِقْدِ ... وذَاتَ اللِّثاثِ الجُمِّ والفاحِمِ الجَعْدِ
(O be safe, lady of the bracelets and necklace, lady of the abundant gums and the black curly hair.)
and his saying:
364 - ألا يا اسْلمي يا هندُ هندَ بني بدرٍ ... وإن كان حَيَّانا عِداً آخرَ الدهرِ
(O be safe, Hind, Hind of the Banū Badr, even if our two clans are enemies to the end of time.)
and his saying:
3565 - ألا يا اسْقِياني قبلَ حَبْلِ أبي بكرِ ... لعل منايانا قَرُبْنَ ولا نَدْري
(O give me drink before the rope of Abū Bakr; perhaps our deaths are near and we do not know.)
and his saying:
3566 - ألا يا اسْقِياني قبلَ غارةِ سِنْجالِ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(O give me drink before the raid of Sinjāl …)
and his saying:
3567 - فقالَتْ ألا يا اسْمَعْ أَعِظْكَ لخُطْبةٍ ... فقلتُ: سَمِعْنا فانْطِقي وأَصِيْبي
(She said, "O listen, I will admonish you with a speech." I said, "We are listening; speak and be right.")
And that has come even where «ألا» does not precede it, as in his saying:
3568 - يا دارَ هندٍ يا اسْلَمي ثُمَّ اسْلَمي ... بِسَمْسَِمٍ أو عَنْ يمين سَمْسَِمِ
(O abode of Hind, O be safe, then be safe, at Samsam or to the right of Samsam.)
You have known, then, that al-Kisāʾī's reading is strong because of the frequency of its occurrence in their language.
It has also been heard in prose; some have been heard saying: «ألا يا ارحموني» and «ألا يا تَصَدَّقوا علينا». As for the saying of another:
3569 - يا لعنةَ اللهِ والأقوامِ كلِّهمُ ... والصالحينَ على سَمْعانَ مِنْ جارِ
(O curse of Allah, and of all peoples and the righteous, upon Samʿān, as a neighbour!)
it is possible that «يا» is for the vocative with the one addressed omitted, and possible that it is for alerting, which is the more preferred for what has passed.
Know that for al-Kisāʾī, pausing at «يَهْتَدون» is a complete pause. He may pause on «ألا يا» together and begin «اسْجُدوا» with a hamza with ḍamma, and he may pause on «ألا» alone and on «يا» alone, because they are two separate particles. These two pauses are pauses of testing, not of choice, because they are two particles whose meaning is not complete except with what they are attached to; the readers did that only for examination and clarity. This, then, is the justification of al-Kisāʾī's reading, and the matter in it is easy.
As for the reading of the others, it needs close examination. There are many possibilities in it. The first: that the original of «ألاَّ» is «أَنْ لا», so «أنْ» is the particle governing the verb after it, and for that reason the nūn of the nominative dropped, and «لا» after it is a negative particle. And «أنْ» and what follows it are in the position of the object of «يَهْتَدون» by removal of the preposition, i.e. "to that they not / prostrate". And «لا» is redundant, like its redundancy in {لِّئَلاَّ يَعْلَمَ أَهْلُ الكتاب} [al-Ḥadīd: 29]. The second: that it is a badal from «أعمالَهم», with a parenthesis between them, the implied form being: "and Satan made the non-prostration to Allah attractive to them". The third: that it is a badal from «السبيل», also with «لا» redundant. The implied form is: "and he turned them away from prostration to Allah the Exalted". The fourth: that {أَلاَّ يَسْجُدُواْ} is a mafʿūl lahu (object of purpose). There are two views about what it is attached to: the first, that it is attached to «زَيَّن», i.e. "he made it attractive to them so that they not prostrate"; the second, that it is attached to «صَدَّهم», i.e. "he turned them away so that they not prostrate". In «لا» then there are two views: the first, that it is not redundant, but negative in its sense of negation; the second, that it is redundant, the meaning being: "he made it attractive to them because of his expecting their prostration, or because of his fear of their prostration". Non-redundancy is more apparent.
The fifth: that it is the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ. This mubtadaʾ is either implied as a pronoun referring to «أعمالَهم», the implied form being "it is that they not prostrate", so that «لا» is in its ordinary sense of negation; or implied as a pronoun referring to «السبيل», the implied form being "it is that they not prostrate", so that «لا» is redundant as previously stated, for the meaning to be sound.
On the four previous possibilities pausing at «يَهْتدون» is not allowed, because what follows it is either governed by it or by what precedes it, namely «زَيَّن» and «صَدَّ», or a badal of what precedes, from «أعمالَهم» or from «السبيل», as established and refined; unlike the fifth possibility, which is built on an implied mubtadaʾ, even if that pronoun is explained by what precedes it.
«ألاَّ» was written joined, not separated, so «أنْ» was not written separately from «لا». For that reason it is not allowed for these readers, in testing and examination, to pause on «أنْ» alone, because of its connection with «لا» in writing; rather they pause on «ألاَّ» as a whole. So said the readers. As for the grammarians, whenever they are asked about such a thing they pause, for clarity, at each word separately, out of the necessity of clarity, and its being written joined to «لا» does not prevent that. Then the readers' statement "it was written joined" has looseness and leniency, because the reality of this is that they would write the form of a nūn and join it to «لا», writing it «أَنْلا»; but since it was assimilated into what follows it in pronunciation and its sound went over to the sound of what follows it, they said that out of leniency.
Abū Isḥāq (al-Zajjāj) based a ruling on the two readings: namely the obligation of the prostration of recitation (sujūd al-tilāwa) or its non-obligation. He made it obligatory with al-Kisāʾī's reading, as if because of the command in it, and did not make it obligatory in the reading of the others, for the absence of a command in it. But al-Zamakhsharī did not approve it of him, for he said: "If you ask: is the prostration of recitation obligatory in both readings, or in one of them? I say: it is obligatory in both, one of the two readings being a command to prostrate and the other a censure of the one who leaves it." So what al-Zajjāj mentioned, of the obligation of the prostration with the light form and not with the heavy, is not to be returned to.
I say: it is as if al-Zajjāj took the apparent sense of the command, and its apparent sense is obligation. Were we left with the verse alone, the prostration would be obligatory; but the Sunna indicated its recommendation rather than its obligation. Moreover we say: this is built on another consideration, namely whether this command is the speech of Allah the Exalted, or the speech of the hoopoe quoted from it. If it is the speech of Allah the Exalted, it is said: it entails obligation unless evidence comes to turn it from its apparent sense; and if it is the speech of the hoopoe, which is the apparent sense, there is, in its standing as evidence, a consideration that is not hidden.
Al-Aʿmash read «هَلاَّ» and «هَلا», turning the hamza into hāʾ, with shadda on «لا» and without it; and so it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh. ʿAbd Allāh read «تَسْجُدون» with the tāʾ of address and the nūn of the nominative. It was also read so with yāʾ (third person). Whoever retains the nūn of the nominative, then «ألا» with shadda or without it is for urging (taḥḍīḍ); the lightened one may also be for offering (ʿarḍ), as in «ألا تَنْزِل عندنا نتحدَّث» ("Won't you stay with us so we may talk?"). In the version of ʿAbd Allāh also: «ألا هَلْ تَسْجدُون» in the second person.
His saying: {الذي يُخْرِجُ الخبء}: It may be in the genitive position as a naʿt of it, or a badal from it, or a bayān; or accusative / for praise; or nominative as the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ. Al-khab' is the maṣdar of «خَبَأْتُ الشَيءَ أخبَؤُه خَبْئاً», i.e. I concealed it; then it was applied to the thing concealed. Like it is {هذا خَلْقُ الله} [Luqmān: 11]. In the exegesis: the concealed in the heavens is the rain, and in the earth the plants. Al-khābiya (the jar) is from this, except that they kept to dropping the hamza in it, like al-bariyya and al-dhurriyya according to some. Ubayy and ʿĪsā read «الخَبَ», transferring the vowel of the hamza to the bāʾ and dropping the hamza, so it becomes like «رأيتُ الأَبَ». ʿAbd Allāh, ʿIkrima and Mālik ibn Dīnār read «الخبا» with a clear alif. Its justification: he turned the hamza into alif, so the bāʾ had to be vowelled; that is according to the dialect of those of the Arabs who, in pausing, replace the hamza with a letter homogeneous with its vowel, so he says «هذا الخَبُوْ», «رأيتُ الخَبا» and «مررت بالخَبِي», and then connected speech was treated as pausing.
In my view, when he transferred the vowel of the hamza to the quiescent letter before it, he did not drop it; rather he left it, so it became quiescent after a fatḥa and was turned according to the vowel of what precedes it; and this is an established dialect: they say «المَراة» and «الكَماة» with an alif in place of the hamza in this way.
Abū Ḥātim attacked this reading and said: "It is not allowed in Arabic, because if he drops the hamza he casts its vowel onto the bāʾ and says «الخَبَ»; and if he converts it he says «الخَبْيَ» with sukūn on the bāʾ and a yāʾ after it." Al-Mubarrad said: "Abū Ḥātim was below his peers in grammar and did not catch up with them, except that when he left their city he met no one more knowledgeable than he."
His saying: {فِي السماوات}: There are two views. The first: it is attached to «الخَبْءَ», i.e. "the hidden in the heavens". The second: it is attached to «يُخْرِجُ», with «في» having the meaning of «مِنْ», i.e. "He brings it out from the heavens". This is al-Farrāʾ's view.
His saying: {مَا تُخْفُونَ}: Al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ read with tāʾ (second person) in both places, and the others with yāʾ (third person). The second person is evident in al-Kisāʾī's reading, because before it is the command to them to prostrate and the addressing of them with it. The third person in the reading of the others, besides Ḥafṣ, is also evident, because the third person pronouns precede, in His sayings «لهم», «أعمالهم», «صَدَّهم» and «فهمْ». As for Ḥafṣ's reading, its interpretation is that he moved on to addressing those present after completing the case of the people of Saba'. It may also be an iltifāt, on the basis that he put the absent in the place of the present and addressed him, turning to him.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The reading with the yāʾ of the third person gives that the verse is from the speech of the hoopoe, and with the tāʾ of address it gives that it is Allah's address to the community of Muḥammad ﷺ." It has already been covered that the apparent sense is that it is the speech of the hoopoe in every case. Likewise the disagreement over His saying {الله لاَ إله إِلاَّ هُوَ}: is it from the speech of the hoopoe, as a correction from it when it described the great throne of Bilqīs, or from the speech of Allah the Exalted, in reply to it in its describing her throne as great?
